content.thinking:
I'm tracing the symptom of shop metrics suddenly going absent, even though the service itself kept serving normally according to logs — so this looks like a monitoring blind spot rather than an outage. I'm building out the causal chain starting with metrics from io-shop halting at a specific timestamp, triggering a MetricsAbsent alert.

The deploy at 11:36 lines up exactly with the onset of the gap, and one candidate explains it as a port rename, but I need to flag that the record itself doesn't confirm this mechanism — it's just a hypothesis tied to coincidental timing, with an unverified PR referenced as the proposed fix. Since the service kept rendering normally with only client-disconnect errors, I'm concluding the failure is isolated to metrics collection rather than the actual service, with the root cause being deploy-related but the exact mechanism still unconfirmed.

For contributing factors, I'm noting there's no existing check ensuring a deploy keeps scrape targets functioning — that needs its own action item, along with a detection gap since alerting only fired well after the actual onset.

Argus had no built-in mitigation path for this failure type, so that's another gap, and since the service was never independently verified while metrics were blind, I want an action item for synthetic probes or log-based health checks. I'm numbering new action items AI-2 through AI-4: preventing recurrence by tying scrape-target checks to deploys, detecting via alerts on targets-down correlated with deploys, and mitigating by verifying scrape config matches real service ports post-merge, plus giving Argus an actual mitigation path like a deploy revert option. I also need to remember not to write raw digits like "11:36" directly in prose — I should reference the placeholder instead.

Reviewing lessons learned: what went well is that Argus quickly pinpointed deploy timing and used logs to separate service health from monitoring health, leading to an opened draft PR. What went wrong is the service was still unobserved at close, with no real health data for the window and an unknown error rate. We got a bit lucky that logs showed normal rendering, but there's a risk a real outage could have been hidden by the monitoring blindness — I'm noting that the log evidence only showed a handful of occurrences in a narrow window. I also want to flag my assumptions clearly: the port-rename mechanism is unconfirmed, error rate is unknown, PR contents weren't reviewed, and log-based health is only partial. For the executive summary, I'll stick to placeholders and avoid any numeric figures entirely.

action_items.item: Add a deploy-time check, and a CI check, that every port or label the scrape config selects on still exists on the deployed service, so a rename fails the pipeline or is changed together with the scrape config.
Add a post-deploy alert that fires when the shop's scrape target disappears or reports down. It should name the most recent deploy so the cause is visible at once.

After the fix merges, confirm that the scraper has the shop as a live target and that samples are arriving again. Record the confirmation on the incident, since it closed with the shop still unobserved.
Give Argus a reviewed mitigation for scrape-target loss after a deploy, such as proposing a rollback of the deploy or applying the scrape-config correction, with human approval.
Add an external synthetic probe or log-based health signal for the shop that does not depend on the metrics pipeline. Use it to judge service health when metrics are absent.

causal_chain.step: Metrics from the shop stopped arriving. The last sample was {T5.2}, and the MetricsAbsent alert fired at {alert_raised} after a gap with no sample ({A2}). The shop was unobserved for {duration} and was still unobserved when the incident closed.

The metrics stopped at the minute a production deploy landed. Deploy {P2.1} went out at the onset {unobserved_from}. The earlier deploy {P1.1} was hours before and did not coincide with the gap. This points to the change as the trigger for the loss of collection.

The shop itself kept serving, so the fault was in collection and not in the service. Logs through and after the onset show pages rendering normally and only client-side disconnects as errors. The flag provider showed no recent flag changes that could explain a change in behaviour.

The scraper therefore lost its target for the shop when the deploy changed it. The most likely mechanism is a renamed metrics port that the scrape config still selected by its old name. The record does not confirm this. The proposed fix in the draft pull request was not verified before the incident closed.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing in the deploy process verified that the shop was still being scraped. A change to the service's metrics port could ship without a matching change to the scrape config, or any check that the target was still discovered.
Detection relied on the metrics going absent. The alert fired only after the gap had grown, and nothing tied the loss of the scrape target to the deploy that caused it.
Argus has no mitigation that answers a monitoring-collection failure. It could only open a draft pull request, so collection stayed broken until a person reviews and merges the fix.
With metrics gone there was no independent signal of shop health. The only evidence was sparse log lines, so a real outage would have been hidden by the blind spot.

input.executive_summary: Monitoring for the shop went blind. Metrics stopped arriving at {unobserved_from}, the same minute a routine production deploy went out. The shop was still unobserved when the incident closed, so for {duration} nobody could see its health through metrics. Logs from that period show normal page rendering and only shoppers closing their own connections, so the shop itself looks to have kept working. Metrics cannot confirm that, and no error rate is known for the window. Argus found no safe action it could take on its own. It handed the work to a person by opening a draft pull request with a proposed fix, and the incident was escalated {closed}. The fix still needs review and merging.

got_lucky: The logs suggest the shop kept serving normally while it was unobserved. If the deploy had also broken the shop, the blind spot would have hidden it, and nothing would have shown the harm.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert within moments and tied the onset to the deploy that landed at the same minute.
Reading the logs separated a monitoring failure from a service failure, which kept the response from chasing a shop outage that the logs do not show.
Argus did not take a mitigation that did not fit this failure. It opened a draft pull request for a person to review.
went_wrong: The shop was still unobserved when the incident closed, and no error rate exists for the window.
The loss of scraping was not caught before the deploy shipped, or at the moment it landed.
The mechanism behind the loss was never verified. The leading candidate was never tried and the fix has not been confirmed to restore metrics.

input.root_cause: The production deploy {P2.1} landed at the exact minute the shop's metrics stopped, and the metrics scraper lost its target for the shop. The likely mechanism is that the deploy renamed the metrics port while the scrape config still selected the old name. That mechanism comes from the Investigator's hypothesis. The record does not confirm it. Nothing in the deploy process checked that the shop was still being scraped.
input.symptom: Shop metrics stopped arriving, leaving the shop unobserved
